text: AAFCO Large Breed Dog Growth: the 2026 AAFCO Growth and Reproduction profile for dogs with its lower calcium max, 4.5 g/Mcal (1.8% DM) instead of 6.25 g/Mcal (2.5% DM). The 2026 AAFCO applies this max to formulas that may be fed to large size puppies, those weighing 70 lb (about 31.8 kg) or more as mature lean adults (Footnote d, page 167; Footnote e, page 165), and, unless a product's labeling restricts it to specific breeds, to products bearing an All Life Stages claim based on being formulated to the Growth and Reproduction profile (page 170); for other life stages, including non-large-breed growth formulas, the calcium max is 6.25 g/Mcal (2.5% DM), as under AAFCO Dog Growth (Small & Medium) and Reproduction. Large size dog growth products and all life stages products substantiated by AAFCO feeding protocols using non-large size dogs must also contain no more than the large size calcium and phosphorus maxs (pages 162 and 186). In this checker the two AAFCO dog growth requirements differ only in this calcium max and in the energy (this one covers growth only; see note n040). The expected mature body weight (mature_weight_kg) is not used by the AAFCO requirements, so choose this requirement for a puppy expected to weigh 70 lb (about 31.8 kg) or more as a lean adult, and for an All Life Stages dog food not restricted to specific breeds (see note n173).

text: Where 0.000000001 is added to a maximum of NRC RA Dog Maintenance, it represents a 2006 NRC adult dog maintenance safe upper limit (SUL) given as a greater-than value; the amount added is clinically insignificant and far beyond any measurable precision. The same rule is used for every NRC greater-than SUL. Used for sodium only: 15/4 + 0.000000001 = 3.750000001 g/Mcal, from >15 g/kg DM in 2006 NRC Table 15-5. The sodium MBW max, 0.4913 (derived from >15 g/kg DM; see note n117), carries no addition, as it is this checker's own estimate, not a limit NRC prints. Iodine (per Mcal and MBW) has no addition, as NRC prints that SUL as >=4 mg/kg DM, not >4. A value equal to the limit itself falls in the top band (range-d10) with or without the addition; because values are compared at 7 decimal places, the addition does not change the band of any entered value. The MBW maximums of this requirement (fat, linoleic acid, EPA + DHA, sodium, chloride, iodine, retinol, vitamin A and vitamin D; the sodium, chloride and iodine ones are this checker's estimates, see their notes) are kept as printed in 2006 NRC Table 15-5 per kg BW^0.75. This checker converts them at the reference energy, NRC's 130 * BW^0.75 (the average laboratory or active dog), whatever the dog type, intake or restriction (the provisional steward's rule), so they equal the per Mcal SULs within about 4%: e.g., the fat MBW max (10.8 g/kg BW^0.75) converts to about 83.1 g/Mcal, against the 82.5 g/Mcal fat SUL. Maximums thus follow the calories fed: a very active dog eating 200 kcal/kg BW^0.75 at 82.5 g fat/Mcal takes in 16.5 g fat/kg BW^0.75 a day, above NRC's 10.8. Table 15-5 Footnote b (page 360) asks for the per kg BW^0.75 amounts for dogs with an unusually low energy intake, which the MBW minimums give (see note n192).

text: For FEDIAF Dog (MER 95 kcal/kg^0.75) and FEDIAF Dog (MER 110 kcal/kg^0.75): the MBW rows of these two requirements hold the FEDIAF Sept. 2025 Table VII-11 (page 58) minimums per kg BW^0.75 for adult dog maintenance, as printed; FEDIAF gives one adult dog column for both MERs. Units are converted where this checker's unit differs (chloride 0.04 g = 40 mg, magnesium 0.02 g = 20 mg, cobalamin 0.92 mcg = 0.00092 mg); folic acid is divided by 0.6 to mcg DFE (=7.1/0.6), as on the folate row; and retinol is the vitamin A IU * 0.3, as on the retinol row. This checker converts them to per Mcal at the energy fed: with no intake or restriction entered they give about the per Mcal values (e.g., protein 4.95 * 1,000/110 = 45 g/Mcal under MER 110), and at a lower energy fed (an intake entered, or a restriction) they give the concentration FEDIAF calls for at that intake (FEDIAF section 7.2.5, pages 59-60: units/1,000 kcal = nutrient requirement per day per kg metabolic BW * 1,000 / energy intake per kg metabolic BW). Table VII-11 is rounded to 2 decimal places, so some converted values differ from the per Mcal values (e.g., sodium 0.03 * 1,000/95 = 0.3158 g/Mcal versus 0.29 g/Mcal; figures rounded; the rounding is clinically insignificant and far beyond any measurable precision). Each MBW row and its per Mcal row are checked separately, so a diet meets both only when it meets the higher one. Table VII-11 gives minimums only. For the 13 MBW rows whose per Mcal row has a max (calcium, phosphorus, sodium, chloride, iron, copper, manganese, zinc, iodine, selenium, retinol, vitamin A and vitamin D), the MBW row's max is this checker's own calculation, not a FEDIAF value: the per Mcal max * the MER / 1,000, the relation of FEDIAF section 7.2.5 applied to a max (e.g., vitamin D 800 * 95/1,000 = 76 IU/kg BW^0.75 under MER 95). It is converted back to per Mcal at the reference energy, FEDIAF's MER, so both rows' ranges end at the same max whatever the intake or restriction (the provisional steward's rule). Its type is CALC (see note n027): a value above it falls in the top band (range-d10), and the Open Animal Nutrition FHIR IG does not call it excess. The other MBW rows have no max (range high 4 times the min). Fat MBW reads none: FEDIAF states that the fat minimum for a MER of 95 kcal/kg BW^0.75 has not been adjusted for energy intake (page 23), and Table VII-11's 1.51 g/kg BW^0.75 fits the MER 110 value only (13.75 * 0.110 = 1.5125). The Selenium, Se MBW row uses the dry diet value (5.20 mcg/kg BW^0.75) for every food; Table VII-11's wet diet value (6.40) is not used, as there is no Selenium, Se (For >12% Moisture Foods) MBW row (see note n257). So with an energy fed below the MER, a food of more than 12% moisture can be asked for up to about 19% less selenium than FEDIAF's wet diet value gives at that intake (5.20 versus 6.40): e.g., under MER 110 at 80 kcal/kg BW^0.75, FEDIAF's equation gives 80 mcg/Mcal for a wet diet (6.40 * 1,000/80), while this checker asks 65 on the MBW row (5.20 * 1,000/80) and 57.5 on the >12% moisture per Mcal row.

text: Maximums of FEDIAF Dog (MER 95 kcal/kg^0.75) (FEDIAF Sept. 2025 Tables III-3a and III-3b, pages 15 and 16): FEDIAF gives nutritional maximums (N) and EU legal maximums (L). This checker uses the nutritional maximum wherever FEDIAF gives one, and the legal maximum only where it gives none; the sodium and chloride maximums are FEDIAF's Footnote c safe levels (see their notes). A legal maximum applies only when that trace element or vitamin is added to the recipe as an additive, and then to the total amount in the food; when it comes only from feed materials, the legal maximum does not apply, and only a nutritional maximum, where FEDIAF gives one, does (section 3.1.3, page 11). FEDIAF gives no nutritional maximum for copper, iodine, iron, manganese, selenium or zinc, so for these the legal maximum is used here for every diet, supplemented or not, as this checker's cautious choice. FEDIAF gives the legal maximums per kg dry matter (DM) only, as they do not account for energy density (page 13); per 100 g DM: copper 2.80 mg, iodine 1.10 mg, iron 68.18 mg, manganese 17.00 mg, selenium 56.80 mcg and zinc 22.70 mg. They are converted at 4 kcal ME/g DM (e.g., iron (681.8/(4*1000))*1000 = 170.45 mg/Mcal), so each equals the legal maximum only for a food of 4 kcal ME/g DM: for a food of 5 kcal ME/g DM the iron legal maximum is 136.36 mg/Mcal, and for a food of 3.5 kcal ME/g DM it is 194.8 mg/Mcal. To check a food against a legal maximum, compare its amount per kg DM. For vitamin D, FEDIAF gives both: this checker uses the nutritional maximum, 800 IU/1,000 kcal ME (320 IU/100 g DM), which FEDIAF sets for growing giant breed dogs and recommends for the other life stages (page 26; it considers 425 IU/100 g DM safe for small breed puppies); when vitamin D is added as an additive, the EU legal maximum of 227 IU/100 g DM (567.5 IU/Mcal at 4 kcal ME/g DM) applies as well. The MBW rows' maximums are not FEDIAF values: each is the per Mcal max * the MER / 1,000, calculated by this checker (type CALC; see note n004).

text: For NRC RA Cat Maintenance: per 2006 NRC Table 15-12 Footnote c (page 367), the Amt/kg BW^0.67 values have been calculated for a lean cat with an energy intake of 100 * BWkg^0.67; for adult cats that are not lean, NRC calculates the amount of a nutrient as the energy requirement from Table 15-11 (see note n032) multiplied by the Amt/1,000 kcal and divided by 1,000, which is what the per Mcal rows give. This checker keeps the MBW values for both cat types: with the overweight equation (130 * BWkg^0.4), the MBW rows convert to about 1.12 to 1.35 times the per Mcal values for cats of 4 to 8 kg (0.769 * BWkg^0.27; figures rounded; the rounding is clinically insignificant and far beyond any measurable precision), so for an overweight cat they ask more than the per Mcal rows. Per Footnote b, cats with an unusually low energy intake (below the suggested requirement) should be fed the Amt/kg BW^0.67 amounts, which the MBW rows give: their minimums are converted at the energy fed (the calculated requirement less any restriction, or the intake entered). Their maximums are converted at NRC's lean cat energy for every cat type (see note n009).

This checker uses the nutritional maximum wherever FEDIAF gives one, and the legal maximum only where it gives none; the sodium maximum is FEDIAF's Footnote e safe level (see its note). A legal maximum applies only when that trace element or vitamin is added to the recipe as an additive, and then to the total amount in the food; when it comes only from feed materials, the legal maximum does not apply, and only a nutritional maximum, where FEDIAF gives one, does (section 3.1.3, page 11). FEDIAF gives no nutritional maximum for copper, iodine, iron, manganese, selenium or zinc, so for these the legal maximum is used here for every diet, supplemented or not, as this checker's cautious choice. FEDIAF gives the legal maximums per kg dry matter (DM) only, as they do not account for energy density (page 13); per 100 g DM: copper 2.80 mg, iodine 1.10 mg, iron 68.18 mg, manganese 17.00 mg, selenium 56.80 mcg and zinc 22.70 mg. They are converted at 4 kcal ME/g DM (e.g., iron (681.8/(4*1000))*1000 = 170.45 mg/Mcal), so each equals the legal maximum only for a food of 4 kcal ME/g DM: for a food of 5 kcal ME/g DM the iron legal maximum is 136.36 mg/Mcal, and for a food of 3.5 kcal ME/g DM it is 194.8 mg/Mcal. To check a food against a legal maximum, compare its amount per kg DM. For vitamin D, FEDIAF gives both: this checker uses the nutritional maximum, 7,500 IU/1,000 kcal ME (3,000 IU/100 g DM), which FEDIAF considers safe for cats of all life stages (page 31); when vitamin D is added as an additive, the EU legal maximum of 227 IU/100 g DM (567.5 IU/Mcal at 4 kcal ME/g DM) applies as well. For the vitamin D2 row, see note n265. The MBW rows' maximums are not FEDIAF values: each is the per Mcal max * the MER / 1,000, calculated by this checker (type CALC; see note n012).

text: For NRC RA Cat Late Gestation: in 2006 NRC Table 15-14 only protein, the amino acids and taurine have separate late gestation values; the fat, fatty acid, mineral and vitamin rows are given for lactating queens only. Per Footnote a, few data could be found on minimal requirements for gestation in the queen except for the amino acids, and the lactation values per kg DM and per 1,000 kcal may be used for gestation as well. Per Footnote d, the printed lactation Amt/kg BW^0.67 values only apply to a 4 kg queen in peak lactation (3-4 kittens, 540 kcal ME/day), and late gestation requirements are calculated from the late gestation ME requirement of 140 * BWkg^0.67 (see note n049) multiplied by the Amt/1,000 kcal and divided by 1,000. So from fat to choline, each MBW value of this requirement (where one is given) is the per Mcal value * 0.14 (except vitamin K; see note n155), not the peak lactation value printed in Table 15-14 (e.g., fat 22.5 g/Mcal * 0.14 = 3.15 g/kgBW^0.67; fat SUL 82.5 g/Mcal * 0.14 = 11.55 g/kgBW^0.67); the products are not rounded. Protein and the amino acids keep the late gestation values printed in Table 15-14, which are on approximately the same 140 kcal basis (e.g., protein 53 g/Mcal and 7.40 g/kgBW^0.67); for taurine see notes n067 and n078. The MBW maximums (fat, linoleic acid, retinol, vitamin A and vitamin D) are likewise the per Mcal SULs * 0.14; this checker converts them at the reference energy, the late gestation requirement (140 * BWkg^0.67), whatever the intake or restriction, so they equal the per Mcal SULs. 2006 NRC prints no late gestation SUL: Table 15-14 (page 369) gives its SULs once, for lactation, and Footnote d's 140 * BWkg^0.67 is for calculating requirements. So these five maximums are this checker's conversions, not NRC SULs, and their type is CALC (see note n027): a value above them falls in the top band (range-d10), and the Open Animal Nutrition FHIR IG does not call it excess.

text: The type of each maximum (max_type in the standards data; blank where the max is none). SUL = a 2006 NRC safe upper limit (SUL) as printed, per Mcal or converted by NRC's own unit factors. SUL> = a 2006 NRC SUL printed as a lower bound: a greater-than value, entered with the 0.000000001 addition, or, for adult dog iodine, ">= 4 mg" per kg DM, entered without it (see notes n003, n009, n015, n017 and n021). SULm and SULm> = the same, per kg metabolic body weight (MBW), converted to per Mcal at the reference energy at the current body weight (see note n003); no maximum is coded SULm> in this data. SULm* = a 2006 NRC SUL per kg MBW that NRC states only for its reference animal, used here for every animal of that requirement: the MBW maximums of NRC RA Kitten Growth (see note n020) and NRC RA Cat Peak Lactation (see note n025). PSM = a presumed safe maximum given in the 2006 NRC text, not in its tables (choline, page 233; see note n164). AAFCO = a 2026 AAFCO profile maximum. N = a FEDIAF Sept. 2025 nutritional maximum (N). N* = a FEDIAF nutritional maximum used beyond the life stage or animals it is stated for: the FEDIAF Dog Late Growth Ca:P max (see note n103) and the FEDIAF Cat Reproduction arginine, methionine, tryptophan and Ca:P maximums, which FEDIAF Table III-4b states for growth (see notes n057, n058, n059 and n105). L = a FEDIAF Sept. 2025 EU legal maximum (L), given per kg dry matter and applying only to nutrients added as additives (FEDIAF page 11), converted here at 4 kcal ME/g DM (see notes n005 and n011). FSL = a FEDIAF safe level from a table footnote, not marked (N) or (L) (sodium and chloride; see their notes). EST = this checker's own estimate (see the value's note). CALC = calculated by this checker from other limits (see the value's source; for the MBW maximums of NRC RA Cat Late Gestation, see note n024). Two more codes describe range highs this checker sets, not maximums of a standard: TPL = set by this checker (see the row's notes), and K = no max, the range high being the min times the row's multiplier (see note n171). A value above any range high falls in the top band (range-d10) whatever the type, except a low value entered on a row with no min (see note n188); the Open Animal Nutrition FHIR IG uses these types to decide when such a value is called excess (see note n188): N*, SULm*, L and FSL are conditional, so a value above them is never called excess. When a max value or its basis changes, change its max_type in the same edit.

text: AAFCO's nutrient profiles set no energy requirement (the 2026 AAFCO per 1,000 kcal ME values are for maintenance of body weight at an average caloric intake for dogs "of a given optimum weight", Footnote a, page 166), so this checker uses its own estimate, by one rule for the five AAFCO requirements (see note n039): for adult maintenance, the 2006 NRC maintenance energy for the type of adult dog chosen (adult_dog_type), the same value as for NRC RA Dog Maintenance (2006 NRC Table 15-4, page 359); with no dog type chosen, the checker asks for one. For the minimums, the reference energy is NRC's average adult dog energy, 130 * BWkg^0.75, whatever the type (the provisional steward's proposal, as AAFCO states no energy basis). The food allowance for test dogs in the 2026 AAFCO Dog and Cat Food Metabolizable Energy Protocols Method 1: Quantitative Collection Part IV. Food Allowances (page 202), "or the estimated daily energy needs required for maintenance of various weights of dogs (Table 5, 1985 Nutrient Requirements of Dogs, NRC, or 132 kcal ME times body weight in kilograms to the 0.75 power)...", is an allowance for feeding test dogs, not a requirement (1.5% above NRC's average of 130 * BWkg^0.75), so it is not used.

text: From 2006 NRC Table 15-7 145*BWkg^0.75+BWkg * (24*number of puppies b/n1-4 +12*number of puppies b/n5-8) * correction factor for stage of lactation (L); Legend for Variable L: Week 1 Factor: 0.75; Week 2 Factor: 0.95; Week 3 Factor: 1.1; Week 4 Factor: 1.2; after week 4: no factor, as 2006 NRC page 38 gives no estimate beyond week 4 because milk yield varies considerably between individuals after 4 weeks of lactation. 2006 NRC pages 37-38 also show how the per-puppy terms are calculated: daily milk yield of about 1% of the bitch's body weight per puppy for puppies 1-4 and 0.5% for puppies 5-8 (no notable further increase above 8 puppies), times about 1.45 kcal gross energy (GE) per g of milk, divided by a 60% utilization of ME for milk production, gives NRC's 24 and 12 kcal ME per kg BW of the bitch per puppy (1% and 0.5% of BW are 10 and 5 g of milk per kg BW; NRC rounds 1.45/0.60 to 2.42, then 10 x 2.42 and 5 x 2.42 to 24 and 12; the rounding is clinically insignificant and far beyond any measurable precision). Using 3 g/Mcal that equates to (3/1000)*1324= 3.972 g Ca/20 kg body weight (BW) or 0.1986 g calcium/kg BW. Which is far less than the footnote minimum of 0.54 g Ca/kg BW. For a puppy with an expected mature body weight over 25 kg, also enter the value on the "Calcium, Ca (NRC puppies 4 to 14 weeks, expected adult weight over 25 kg)" row, which applies the footnote with the current body weight (body_weight_kg). text: From 2006 NRC, Table 15-5 Footnote i 1 microgram cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) = 40 IU vitamin D3. Morris of UC Davis in 2002 showed that cats used vitamin D2 with an efficiency of 70% as compared to vitamin D3 (J Anim Physiol Anim Nutr (Berl). 2002; 86(7-8):229-38.). The 2006 NRC (page 201) states that in most species vitamin D3 is used with equal or greater efficiency than vitamin D2, citing cats, and does not state this for dogs; but it has been known since 1939 that dogs utilize vitamin D2 and D3 equally well (Arnold and Elvehjem, J Am Vet Med Assoc. 1939; 95:187-194.). In that first definitive study at the University of Wisconsin, growing dogs grew normally, with radiographic (x-ray) monitoring of bone development (if developmental abnormalities appeared) and blood calcium and phosphorus levels, over a five month experimental period. Later in 1943, Morgan and Shimotori of UC Berkeley showed that the same single massive IU dose of either vitamin D2 or vitamin D3 maintained blood calcium levels and vitamin D levels equivalently in growing dogs over the 180 day study (J Biol Chem. 1943; 147:189-200.). It is worth noting that in this study, it appeared that the vitamin D2 may have had a better lasting effect in the last couple of weeks compared to the vitamin D3 sources. Subsequently in 1947, Morgan with colleagues Hendricks and Freytag at UC Berkeley showed normal growth in control dogs over approximately 300 days when the same amount of vitamin D2 or vitamin D3 was fed as part of this vitamin D toxicity study (Am J Physiol. 1947; 149:319-332.). Finally the specific effects of vitamin D toxicity on the adult dog’s kidneys were studied in 1979 by Spangler, Gribble, and Lee at UC Davis. In this study, they used an overdose of vitamin D2 exclusively. This helped to further confirm that the utilization of vitamin D2 is not unique to growing dogs (Am J Vet Res. 1979; 40:73-83.). More recently, adult dogs fed a plant-based diet with vitamin D2 in place of D3 for 3 months maintained serum total vitamin D and bone mineralisation (Dodd et al., Br J Nutr. 2024; 131(3):391-405.). A supportive study in two client-owned dogs was also completed and selected by peers for oral presentation (Delaney SJ. Serum ionized calcium, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and parathyroid hormone in two dogs fed a homemade diet fortified with vitamin D2. Published in the symposium proceedings, J Anim Physiol Anim Nutr 2015;99(5):810-824 (https://doi.org/10.1111/jpn.12390).).

text: No automatic adjustment is made to vitamin E concentrations for high PUFA diets which the 2006 NRC recommends increasing in high PUFA diets. See p. 208 for Table 8-2 and the Muggli 1994 proposed formula to calculate if of interest and/or sources of PUFAs requiring high amounts of additional vitamin E are not already fortified like fish oils rich in EPA and DHA. Also see the possible impact of increased vitamin E on vitamin K in Delaney and Dzanis 2018 DOI: 10.2460/javma.252.5.537 . The 2026 AAFCO indicates for dogs (pages 165 and 167), "A diet containing 50 IU of vitamin E will have a ratio >=0.6:1 when the PUFA content is 83 grams or less. Diets containing more than 83 grams of PUFA should contain an additional 0.6 IU of vitamin E for every gram of PUFA." and for cats (pages 175 and 177), "Add 10 IU vitamin E above the minimum concentration for each gram of fish oil per kilogram of diet." AAFCO's dog figures of 50 IU and 83 grams are amounts per kg of dry matter: 50 IU/kg DM is its dog vitamin E minimum in the dry matter table (page 164), given as 12.5 IU per 1,000 kcal ME in its other table (page 166) at its presumed 4,000 kcal ME/kg DM, so 83 grams of PUFA per kg DM is about 20.8 g per 1,000 kcal ME. The 2006 NRC tables give vitamin E in mg alpha-tocopherol, with the footnote 1 IU = 1 mg all-rac-alpha-tocopheryl acetate (footnotes to Tables 15-3, 15-5, 15-8, 15-10, 15-12 and 15-14, pages 358, 360, 363, 365, 367 and 369, referring to its Chapter 8), and this checker uses the NRC mg as IU one to one (this checker's choice, following that footnote); for dogs this fits the 2006 NRC adequate intake of 24 IU per 4,000 kcal (page 209), the 6.0 mg per 1,000 kcal of Tables 15-3, 15-5 and 15-8 (pages 358, 360 and 363). In IU per mg, relative to all-rac-alpha-tocopheryl acetate (1.00), the 2006 NRC (page 207) gives all-rac-alpha-tocopherol 1.10, RRR-alpha-tocopheryl acetate 1.36, RRR-alpha-tocopherol (the naturally occurring form) 1.49, all-rac-alpha-tocopheryl succinate 0.89 and RRR-alpha-tocopheryl succinate 1.21 (United States Pharmacopeia 1985, largely from studies in rats; not measured in dogs or cats); FEDIAF Sept. 2025 Table VII-14 (page 63) gives the same factors for the alcohol and acetate forms. Enter vitamin E in IU: multiply the mg of a stated form by its factor (e.g., 10 mg RRR-alpha-tocopherol is 14.9 IU). No vitamin E maximum is used, as none of the three standards sets one, so the range high is the min times the row's multiplier (4) and values above it fall in the top band (range-d10). The 2006 NRC states that there is no information on vitamin E toxicity in dogs, that Hall et al. (2003) gave dogs 447 mg all-rac-tocopheryl acetate for 17 weeks with no adverse effects (no basis, such as per kg diet, is printed for this amount) and that the NRC (1987) suggested a maximum tolerable level of 1,000 to 2,000 IU/kg diet (page 209). For cats it reports dose-related toxicity of vitamin E injected into kittens from birth to 3 weeks of age (no deaths at about 20 mg/kg BW/day, significant mortality at 100 to 200 mg/kg BW/day and death of all kittens at 1,000 mg/kg BW/day; Phelps 1981; the 2006 NRC also describes the injected doses as about 50 to 1,000 mg/kg BW/day, a range the 20 mg/kg BW/day figure lies below: an inconsistency in NRC's text, kept here as printed) and prolonged clotting times, restored by vitamin K therapy, in cats fed fish-based diets fortified with vitamin E (Strieker et al. 1996), and it concludes that the data do not allow a safe upper limit of vitamin E to be defined (pages 209 and 210). The 2026 AAFCO records that the dog vitamin E maximum was deleted from its profiles because the 2006 NRC had set no safe upper limit, having no information on vitamin E toxicity in dogs (page 173). See also Delaney and Dzanis 2018 on the possible impact of increased vitamin E on vitamin K (DOI: 10.2460/javma.252.5.537).

text: NRC, AAFCO, and FEDIAF report "folic acid" requirements and not folate; 1 mcg DFE (dietary folate equivalent) = 1 mcg food folate per the US NIH (https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Folate-HealthProfessional/ accessed 23SEP25); folate is the vitamin B9 water-soluble vitamin naturally present in foods. Per the NIH: "Folic acid is the fully oxidized monoglutamate form of the vitamin that is used in fortified foods and most dietary supplements." To convert to the common mcg DFE unit that covers all food and fortified/supplemental forms, one divides the Folic Acid value in mcg by 0.6 as 1 mcg DFE = 0.6 mcg folic acid when consumed with food. Every folic acid minimum in this checker (2006 NRC, 2026 AAFCO and FEDIAF Sept. 2025) is converted this way, so each minimum here is the printed folic acid value expressed in mcg DFE: a diet whose folate comes from added folic acid meets it at the printed amount (e.g., the 2026 AAFCO cat minimum of 0.20 mg folic acid/1,000 kcal ME, page 177, is 333.3 mcg DFE/Mcal), while folate naturally present in foods counts one to one, so a diet relying on food folate needs 1.67 times the printed amount. The 2006 NRC states that its vitamin minimums are the bioavailable forms in the diet at the point of consumption, generally adequate when most of a vitamin comes from a vitamin premix, and that when a vitamin comes mainly from food ingredients the minimum should be modified by a suitable factor (Note on Bioavailability, page 356); FEDIAF Sept. 2025 bases its B vitamin minimums on bioavailable forms from a vitamin premix (pages 27 and 31). The 2026 AAFCO profiles give folic acid with no form or bioavailability basis (pages 166 and 177); AAFCO set its dog value equal to the 2006 NRC adequate intake (page 173) and kept its cat value at or above the 2006 NRC recommended allowance (page 179). The 0.6 comes from human nutrition (the NIH, above), and none of these standards gives a folate factor for dogs or cats, so dividing every folic acid minimum by 0.6 is this checker's choice, the cautious one when folate comes from food. Enter folate as mcg DFE per Mcal: mcg food folate + (mcg folic acid / 0.6).

text: This is the adequate intake (AI) value as there is no basis for the higher Table 15-5 value of 425 mg/Mcal choline in the 2006 NRC, see page 233 in 2006 NRC where the allowance of 340 mg/Mcal is actually "recommended" for all life stages. The same AI of 340 mg/Mcal is used for the other NRC dog requirements (NRC RA Puppy 4-14 Wk Growth, NRC RA Puppy 14 Wk+ Growth and NRC RA Dog Late Gestation & Peak Lactation), where 2006 NRC Tables 15-3 and 15-8 (pages 358 and 363) also print 340 mg/Mcal as the AI and 425 mg/Mcal as the RA. text: Maximum 500 mg/Mcal for the four NRC dog requirements only (NRC RA Dog Maintenance, NRC RA Puppy 4-14 Wk Growth, NRC RA Puppy 14 Wk+ Growth and NRC RA Dog Late Gestation & Peak Lactation); no NRC, AAFCO or FEDIAF table gives a choline maximum, and none is set for the AAFCO or FEDIAF requirements: 2006 NRC (page 233) proposes "a presumed safe maximum intake of 2,000 mg choline·kg-1 diet", converted here at 4,000 kcal ME/kg and used as an authoritative maximum until better safety data, including data with controls, are available. When 1.1 times the higher of the choline minimum and the choline MBW minimum (converted to per Mcal) is above 500, that value is the maximum instead, of type TPL, so a value above it is never called excess (the provisional steward's rule, 23 Oct 2026): no standard sets a choline maximum from controlled safety data, so a range of at least 10% is kept above the minimum (calcium, whose tight control has data behind it, keeps its narrow range; see note n234). Note the inconsistency: the study NRC cites for this level, McKibbin et al. NRC (page 233) also notes that only Davis (1944a,b), with no control dogs, reported anemia in dogs given choline (Davis 1944, Am J Physiol 142:65-67 and 142:402-406; see also Davis 1947, Science 105:43-44), and that in pigs 2,000 mg/kg diet decreased weight gain when fed from weaning (Southern et al. 1986). text: Enter values for the whole daily ration as eaten, including any treats and anything added to the food, not for one part of it: FEDIAF Sept. 2025 (page 32), on complementary pet foods, states that the total daily ration should match the recommended allowances and the nutritional and legal maximum values listed for complete pet food. This checker applies no processing loss, bioavailability or digestibility factor, except the folate DFE conversion (see note n161) and the cat vitamin D2 min (see note n264), so values calculated from a recipe or from ingredient composition data need such allowances before they are entered (see notes n258 and n274). Under the 2026 AAFCO, iron from carbonate or oxide sources and copper from oxide sources that are added to the diet should not be counted toward the iron and copper mins, because of very poor digestibility or bioavailability (pages 165, 167, 175 and 177; see notes n246 and n248). text: Each row has a multiplier that derives the range high from the min when there is no SUL or max: 4, unless the row's notes give another factor. A range high derived this way (the min times the multiplier) is this checker's banding device, not a max or a safe upper limit (code K in note n027; the Open Animal Nutrition FHIR IG calls it derived-provisional and never calls a value above it excess). That a standard sets no max does not mean that higher intakes are safe: the 2026 AAFCO (page 163) states that the absence of a maximum concentration should not be interpreted to mean that nutrients without a specific maximum content are safe at any concentration, as it reflects the lack of information in dogs and cats on toxic concentrations of that nutrient, and the 2006 NRC (page 354) states that SUL values are not available for many required nutrients, especially minerals and vitamins. For potassium, the 2026 AAFCO (page 170) did not establish a maximum for dogs because potential toxicosis of potassium was not a practical concern. A value above such a range high falls in the top band (range-d10), as does a value from 90% of the range up to it; neither description shows the value to be safe or excessive.

text: What the values in this table are, and what a band does and does not show. The mins and maxs are the selected requirement's values, in each row's unit (per Mcal on most rows; see note n187), or this checker's own where its notes say so; they are not all minimum requirements. The 2006 NRC requirements use recommended allowances (RA; except where a row's notes say otherwise), which NRC defines as the concentration or amount of a nutrient in a diet formulated to support a given physiological state; the RA is based on the minimal requirement (MR) and, where applicable, includes a safety factor for nutrients with uncertain bioavailability, and where no MR is available, the RA is based on the adequate intake (AI) (2006 NRC page 354). The 2026 AAFCO profiles were designed to establish practical minimum and some maximum nutrient concentrations for dog and cat foods formulated from commonly used, non-purified, complex ingredients, and these concentrations differ from minimum nutrient requirements (2026 AAFCO page 161). The FEDIAF Sept. 2025 values are minimum recommended nutrient levels for commercial pet food, not minimum requirements or optimal intake levels (FEDIAF Sept. 2025 page 14). So a value below a min is below that standard's recommendation, which is not by itself proof that the diet is inadequate for the animal, and a value at or above every min is not by itself proof of adequacy: the 2026 AAFCO (page 162) states that no list of concentrations can invariably ensure that all nutrient requirements are fulfilled in all diet formulas without additional considerations, and that formulating to a profile should not discourage feeding trials. Products substantiated by AAFCO feeding protocols are not mandated to meet the profile mins or maxs, except that large size dog growth and all life stages products substantiated with non-large size dogs must not exceed the large size calcium and phosphorus maxs (2026 AAFCO page 162), and FEDIAF states that pet foods can be adequate and safe with nutrient levels outside its recommendations, based on the manufacturer's substantiation of nutritional adequacy and safety (FEDIAF Sept. 2025 page 10). Some mins are conditional in the standards (e.g., for cats, the 2026 AAFCO states that vitamin K does not need to be added unless the diet contains more than 25% fish on a DM basis, and biotin unless the diet contains antimicrobial or antivitamin compounds; pages 175 and 177); this checker applies such mins to every diet (see notes n272 and n280). A min or max of "none" means this checker uses no value from the selected requirement for that row: usually the requirement gives none (in the 2006 NRC tables the absence of data marks a gap in knowledge, page 354, and the 2026 AAFCO marks some values ND, not determined, e.g., Footnote c, page 167), and for a few requirements this checker does not use a printed value (see each requirement's notes). With no max, the range high is derived from the min (see note n171); for the kinds of max, see note n188. The bands only compare the entered values with these ranges; they do not check a nutrient's source or form, digestibility, processing losses or what the entered values represent (see note n170).

text: Choosing a requirement: the requirement chosen sets the mins and maxs and the energy (see note n172 for what these values are). Foods for all life stages: FEDIAF Sept. 2025 (page 10) states that a complete food labelled without a specific life stage is assumed to be complete for all life stages and should be formulated according to the levels recommended for early growth and reproduction. For dogs, use FEDIAF Dog Early Growth (< 14 wk) & Reproduction. For cats, FEDIAF combines growth and reproduction in one table and states both values where they differ (page 13); in this checker FEDIAF Cat Reproduction is at least as strict as FEDIAF Cat Growth on every nutrient row (higher protein and arginine mins and a lower vitamin A max; its other nutrient values are the same), so use FEDIAF Cat Reproduction (this checker's reading). The 2026 AAFCO (page 170) states that, unless a product's labeling restricts it to specific breeds, a dog food bearing an All Life Stages claim based on being formulated to its Growth and Reproduction profile should not contain more than 1.8% calcium on a dry matter (DM) basis, the max for formulas that may be fed to large size puppies (see note n002). In this checker AAFCO Large Breed Dog Growth has the values of AAFCO Dog Growth (Small & Medium) and Reproduction except that calcium max (4.5 instead of 6.25 g/Mcal) and its energy (growth only), so check such a food with AAFCO Large Breed Dog Growth (this checker's suggestion). For these food checks, only the energy row needs the animal's facts (see each requirement's energy note) or an intake (energy_intake_kcal_per_day), as these requirements have no MBW values. Low energy foods: the 2026 AAFCO states that formulations of low energy density should not be considered adequate for reproductive needs (dogs), or for growth or reproductive needs (cats), based on comparison to the profiles alone (Footnote a, pages 164 and 175), and that unless a product meeting its definition of a "lite" or "low calorie" product has successfully passed the appropriate AAFCO feeding protocols, it should not be considered adequate for growth or reproduction, regardless of the concentrations of the other nutrients (page 183). Its adult maintenance values are recommended concentrations for maintenance of body weight at an average caloric intake for dogs or cats of a given optimal weight (Footnote a, pages 166 and 177); for a food intended to supply significantly fewer calories than typically consumed by the average animal of that weight and life stage, the 2026 AAFCO states that the concentrations of some nutrients per 1000 kcal ME may need to be increased (page 183; see note n192).

text: Body weight (body_weight_kg): the animal's current body weight in kg, for every animal; for lactating queens, the body weight at mating, as in the 2006 NRC Table 15-13 example (page 368). It is used by every energy equation and every MBW conversion. For growing puppies and kittens the 2006 NRC growth equations also use the "actual body weight at time of evaluation", with the expected mature body weight (mature_weight_kg) (Tables 15-2 and 15-9, pages 356 and 364), as does 2025 FEDIAF Table VII-8b (page 56); a current body weight above the expected mature body weight is reported as an input error. For pregnant and lactating bitches, 2006 NRC Tables 15-6 and 15-7 (page 361) and pages 37-38 do not say at which point body weight is taken. The standards' adult maintenance figures assume an animal at its optimal weight: 2025 FEDIAF bases energy requirements on optimal body weight (section 7.1.1, page 43); the 2026 AAFCO profiles are for dogs "of a given optimum weight" (page 166) and cats "of a given optimal weight" (page 177); and the 2006 NRC maintenance recommendations are calculated for lean adults (pages 355-356). This checker still asks for the current body weight (the provisional steward's rule): a caloric restriction is a cut from what the animal eats at its current weight, and the minimums are set so that the diet supplies the daily amounts for the current weight. When the energy calculated at an optimal weight will be fed, enter that weight as well (optimal_body_weight_kg; adult maintenance only).

text: From 2006 NRC Table 3-5: For PUPPIES - Medium Breeds (mature BW 20 kg) - 1 month (mo): 1.8 kg, 9% of mature BW; 2 mo: 4.4 kg, 22%; 3 mo: 7.4 kg, 37%; 4 mo: 10.4 kg, 52%; 6 mo: 14 kg, 70%; 12 mo: 19 kg, 95% | Large Breeds (mature BW 35 kg) - 1 month (mo): 2.5 kg, 7% of mature BW; 2 mo: 7 kg, 20%; 3 mo: 12.3 kg, 35%; 4 mo: 16.8 kg, 48%; 6 mo: 22.8 kg, 65%; 12 mo: 30.8 kg, 88% | Giant Breeds (mature BW 60 kg) - 1 month (mo): 3.6 kg, 6% of mature BW; 2 mo: 8.4 kg, 14%; 3 mo: 15.6 kg, 26%; 4 mo: 22.8 kg, 38%; 6 mo: 36 kg, 60%; 12 mo: 48 kg, 80% | The expected mature body weight (mature_weight_kg) is also used for KITTENS. 2006 NRC page 38: especially in large and giant breeds, optimal, not maximal, growth is important for proper skeletal development, and "The individual large- or giant-breed puppy should be fed to meet these recommendations rather than being fed according to energy requirement figures" (the weights above); 2025 FEDIAF (page 56) also recommends regular weighing of puppies and individual correction of the food allocation to keep growth along its growth curves. text: The animal's life stage (life_stage), read only by the AAFCO growth requirements and the requirements that cover lactation: AAFCO Dog Growth (Small & Medium) and Reproduction, AAFCO Large Breed Dog Growth, AAFCO Cat Growth and Reproduction, FEDIAF Dog Early Growth (< 14 wk) & Reproduction, FEDIAF Cat Reproduction, NRC RA Dog Late Gestation & Peak Lactation and NRC RA Cat Peak Lactation (see their energy notes); the other requirements ignore it. text: AAFCO dry matter factor: 4 divided by the energy density entered (the low entry of the Energy Density row, in kcal ME/g DM) when an AAFCO requirement is chosen and that entry is above 0 and below 4; otherwise 1. Under an AAFCO requirement this factor multiplies each min that a caloric restriction raises (including the arginine base and the ALA min), and also the fat min, which a restriction does not raise; with both, the two factors multiply (see note n192). text: Type of adult dog: the 2006 NRC daily maintenance energy for adult dogs, in kcal ME per kg BW^0.75 (Table 15-4, page 359): 130, the average for laboratory kennel dogs or active pet dogs (dogs kept in a domestic environment with strong stimulus and ample opportunity to exercise, e.g., in a multiple-dog household in the country or in a house with a large yard); above average, 140 for young adult laboratory or active pet dogs, 180 for adult laboratory or active pet terriers and 200 for adult laboratory or active pet Great Danes; below average, 95 for inactive pet dogs (little stimulus and opportunity to exercise) and 105 for older laboratory or older active pet dogs and for laboratory Newfoundlands. NRC adds that the requirements of older or overweight dogs may still be overestimated (Table 15-4 Footnote b). The type chosen (adult_dog_type) sets the energy of these requirements: NRC RA Dog Maintenance (the type's value * BWkg^0.75; see note n028); AAFCO Dog Maintenance (the same value; AAFCO's profiles set no energy requirement, see note n029); NRC RA Dog Late Gestation & Peak Lactation in late gestation, with None or Gestation: week 5 to birth as the life stage (the type's value * BWkg^0.75 + 26 * BWkg; see note n047); and AAFCO Dog Growth (Small & Medium) and Reproduction in gestation (with Gestation: weeks 1-4, the type's value * BWkg^0.75; with Gestation: week 5 to birth, the late gestation energy above; see note n039). With no type chosen, NRC RA Dog Maintenance and AAFCO Dog Maintenance report that the type is needed (the energy used is then the intake, if one is entered), while the two gestation rules use NRC's average of 130. The type sets only the energy fed: for the limits of NRC and AAFCO adult dogs, the reference energy is NRC's average, 130 * BWkg^0.75, whatever the type (the provisional steward's rule; see note n192), so a type below the average raises the minimums of rows with no MBW minimum (every AAFCO row except fat and the ratios) by 130 divided by the type's value (e.g., about 1.37 for the inactive type). The type is not used by the FEDIAF dog requirements, which use FEDIAF's own energy bases (see notes n030, n031, n041 and n043), by the NRC puppy requirements (their equation uses the average 130 * BWkg^0.75 maintenance term), or for lactation (2006 NRC Table 15-7 uses 145 * BWkg^0.75 for every bitch; see note n047).

text: Type of adult cat: the 2006 NRC daily maintenance energy for adult cats (Table 15-11, page 366): lean domestic cats, with a body condition score of 5 or less on a 9-point scale, 100 kcal * BWkg^0.67; overweight domestic cats, with a body condition score above 5, 130 kcal * BWkg^0.4. text: Intake below the requirement's energy (intake_shortfall in each result's factors): how far the intake entered (energy_intake_kcal_per_day) is below the requirement's calculated energy, as a share of it: (calculated energy - intake) / calculated energy; none when no intake is entered or it is not below. This share sets no limit, but the intake itself does: it is the energy fed, so MBW minimums are converted at it, and, under an adult maintenance requirement, on a row with no MBW minimum (fat and the ratios excepted) the per-Mcal minimum is multiplied by the reference energy divided by the intake when the intake is below the reference, as the standards' per-Mcal figures assume the reference energy (see each result's "How energy sets the limits" text). text: MBW = metabolic body weight; used to indicate when nutrient standard is derived from a MBW requirement on for example a per kgBW^0.75 (dogs) or kgBW^0.67 (cats) basis. On the MBW rows, the selected requirement's value per kg BW^0.75 (dogs) or BW^0.67 (cats) is converted to per Mcal: minimums at the energy fed, maximums at the reference energy (see note n192). The 2006 NRC (pages 355 and 356) notes that the requirements for some minerals may vary more directly with body weight (BW) than with metabolic BW; for those nutrients the requirement per Mcal rises or falls with body size (its Table 15-1 illustrates this: relative to a 15 kg dog, -40% at 2 kg and +61% at 100 kg; relative to a 4 kg lean cat, -20% at 2 kg and +14% at 6 kg), which may need to be considered when making diets for individuals using minimal requirements (MRs) and safe upper limits (SULs). NRC does not name these minerals there; it states that Table 15-1 only illustrates the concept and should not be used to formulate diets, and refers to the footnotes of its Chapter 15 tables for calculating the requirements of dogs and cats of different sizes. text: Mcal = megacalorie = 1,000 kcal of metabolizable energy (ME), as in the NRC, AAFCO and FEDIAF tables. All per-Mcal amounts in this checker (e.g., g/Mcal = g per 1,000 kcal ME) are on this basis, so values entered for those rows need to be per 1,000 kcal ME too. The kcal in the energy and energy density rows are also ME. How a diet's ME is determined changes every per Mcal value entered and the energy density, and so can change a band. The 2026 AAFCO uses the methods specified in its Model Regulation PF9 to determine ME (page 163): its profiles presume 4,000 kcal ME/kg DM determined in accordance with PF9 (Footnote a, pages 164 and 175), a food's energy density is to be determined in accordance with PF9 before correcting for it (page 183), and its worked examples calculate ME with 3.5, 8.5 and 3.5 kcal per g of crude protein, crude fat and nitrogen-free extract (pages 184 and 186). FEDIAF Sept. 2025 regards feeding trials as the most accurate way to measure a food's energy density (page 11) and as the gold standard (page 51); otherwise ME is calculated with the 2006 NRC four-step predictive equations for prepared dog and cat foods, dry and wet, and with 4, 9 and 4 kcal per g (dogs) or 4, 8.5 and 4 kcal per g (cats) of crude protein, crude fat and nitrogen-free extract for products of vegetable or animal origin in their natural state, fresh or preserved, and for highly digestible special products (pages 49 to 51). The 2006 NRC tables give values per 1,000 kcal ME and per kg DM, assuming 4,000 kcal ME per kg DM (page 354). Use the method that fits the requirement chosen, and state it when citing a band (this checker's suggestion). The calculated carbohydrate max uses 4, 9 and 4 kcal per g whichever requirement is chosen (see note n289).

text: For a maximum and its calculation, see the notes on that value and on its row. The type of each max (e.g., a 2006 NRC SUL, a 2026 AAFCO max, a FEDIAF nutritional or legal max, or this checker's own estimate) is recorded with it (max_type); see note n027 for the codes. The kinds of max differ. A 2006 NRC safe upper limit (SUL) is based on the maximal concentration or amount of a nutrient that has not been associated with adverse effects in dogs and cats (2006 NRC page 354); NRC prints some SULs as lower bounds (">" values) and some per kg metabolic body weight (codes SUL>, SULm and SULm>; SULm* where NRC states a per kg SUL only for its reference kitten or queen and this checker uses it for every one), and its choline max for dogs is a presumed safe maximum given in its text (page 233; code PSM; see note n164). The 2026 AAFCO set maxs for nutrients where the potential for overuse or toxicity is of concern; foods that reference its profiles must contain no more than any max listed, and AAFCO states that establishing a maximum concentration implies safety below that concentration for long term consumption (2026 AAFCO pages 162 and 163; code AAFCO). A FEDIAF nutritional maximum (N) is the maximum level of a nutrient in a complete pet food that, based on scientific data, has not been associated with adverse effects in healthy dogs and cats; levels above it may still be safe, but no scientific data are currently known to FEDIAF (FEDIAF Sept. 2025 pages 8 and 11). A FEDIAF legal maximum (L) is an EU limit for nutrients added as additives: it applies only when the nutrient is added to the recipe as an additive, and then to the total amount in the food, and FEDIAF gives it on a dry matter basis only (page 11). A FEDIAF footnote safe level (FSL: sodium under the FEDIAF requirements, and chloride under the FEDIAF dog requirements) is a level that a FEDIAF table footnote states to be safe, without marking it (N) or (L) (FEDIAF Sept. 2025 page 21; see note n240 and note n027). Other range highs are this checker's: its own estimates or calculations (codes EST, CALC and TPL; see the value's or row's notes), or, when there is no max, the min times the row's multiplier (code K; see note n171). On a row with a min, whatever the kind of max, a value above the range high falls in the top band (range-d10), as does a value from 90% of the range up to it; on a row with a max but no min, only a high entry is banded, and a low entry is reported as "No minimum for this requirement." (see note n189). For the Open Animal Nutrition FHIR IG these kinds are grouped as follows (proposed, pending ratification): authoritative (SUL, SUL>, SULm, SULm>, PSM, AAFCO and N), the only kind above which the IG calls a value excess; conditional (L, FSL, N* and SULm*, the last two being a FEDIAF or NRC max used beyond the life stage or reference animal it is stated for, and AAFCO while the AAFCO dry matter factor is above 1, as AAFCO compares a food below 4 kcal/g DM with its dry matter values while the maxs here stay per Mcal; see note n299); template-set (EST, CALC and TPL); and derived-provisional (K).

text: Bands compare each entered value with the min, max and band edges, both rounded to 7 decimal places (the rounding is clinically insignificant and far beyond any measurable precision). Each band runs from its lower edge up to, but not including, the next band's lower edge, so a value equal to a band's lower edge belongs to that band; the first band also takes any value below 0 (e.g., a negative carbohydrate by difference), and the top band takes every value at or above its lower edge. On a row where the requirement chosen gives no range (no max, and no min or no range above the min), a value that would otherwise be banded is reported as "No range" instead, unless it is below a stated min. text: Caloric restriction (caloric_restriction_percent): how far below the animal's energy need the diet is fed, in cases of active and intentional weight loss; enter the percentage as a number, 25 for a 25% restriction. text:
This row applies the 2006 NRC Table 15-3 Footnote h, which the general calcium row does not; it states "The RA for the calcium requirements of weaned puppies (of expected mature body weight >25 kg) for up to 14 weeks of life should not be less than 0.54 g calcium/kg body weight." For example, a 20 kg 14 wk dog (using a giant breed worst case scenario) has an RER of 70*20^0.75 = 662 kcal. Multiplying RER by 2 (due to say early neutering/minimal MER factor for growth to get worst case scenario) = 1324 kcal/day. Using 3 g/Mcal that equates to (3/1000)*1324= 3.972 g Ca/20 kg body weight (BW) or 0.1986 g calcium/kg BW. Which is far less than the footnote minimum of 0.54 g Ca/kg BW. For a puppy with an expected mature body weight over 25 kg, enter the value on this row as well as on the general calcium row; this row applies the footnote with the current body weight (body_weight_kg). On this row, the maximum is 10% more than the minimum when the minimum exceeds the 2006 NRC safe upper limit (SUL) of 4.5 g Ca/Mcal, as it can for some puppies. No 4-14 wk puppy with an expected mature body weight of >25 kg has been extrapolated/derived as the NRC intentionally did not provide an RA on a per kgBW^0.75 basis. Attempts at deriving where BW = 1 kg result in the same per kg BW values as 1^0.75 = 1. Attempts at using 2 kg BW where 2^0.75 = 1.6817 and the dose should be 0.54 g/kg BW (2*0.54=1.08) or 1.08 g for a 2 kg puppy would result in a per kgBW^0.75 value of 0.642/kg BW^0.75 (1.08/1.6817 = 0.642) but this is erroneous mathematically and thus fails at 3 kg BW where 3 kg BW*0.54g/kg BW = 1.62 g and 0.642 g * 3^0.75 = 0.642 * 2.279 = 1.46 g which is less than the linear per kg BW min value set by the NRC. 

This row applies only under NRC RA Puppy 4-14 Wk Growth with an expected mature body weight (mature_weight_kg) over 25 kg; otherwise its min and max are not computed. Its min is the larger of 3 g/Mcal and 0.54 g Ca/kg BW times the current body weight (body_weight_kg), divided by the energy in Mcal (kcal/day / 1000). Any caloric restriction adjustment is applied to the 3 g/Mcal min, as for other mins, and to the body-weight min only when no intake is entered: an intake entered is the energy actually fed, so the body-weight min converted with it already supplies 0.54 g/kg BW per day, and applying the adjustment again would count the restriction twice. The max is 4.5 g/Mcal, or 10% more than the min when the min exceeds 4.5. For example, 20 kg at 1324 kcal/day gives (0.54*20)/(1324/1000) = 8.16 g Ca/Mcal, so the max is 8.97 g Ca/Mcal. If the energy cannot be calculated, the min is not computed.

text: For cats, the Vitamin D (dogs: D2 + D3; cats: D3) maximum, unchanged; none for dogs. The ÷0.70 used for the D2 minimum (see note n264) is deliberately not applied to the maximum, despite Morris 2002 (J Anim Physiol Anim Nutr 86(7-8):229-38). Morris found that cats use vitamin D2 with an efficiency of 0.7 of that of vitamin D3 to maintain plasma 25-hydroxyvitamin D: with both forms in the diet in the nutritional range, plasma 25-hydroxyvitamin D2 was 0.68 of 25-hydroxyvitamin D3, and after a single oral bolus of 337 micrograms of each form, peak plasma ergocalciferol was less than half that of cholecalciferol. That is why the D2 minimum is higher, and it makes it plausible that D2 is also less potent at high intakes; but these are plasma measurements at nutritional intakes or after one dose, and they do not show how much D2 is safe with sustained intake near the maximum. The cat maximums are safety limits stated as, or based on, vitamin D3: the 2006 NRC states its safe upper limit as cholecalciferol, the 2026 AAFCO (page 179) bases its maximum on Sih et al. 2001 and the NRC limit, and the 2025 FEDIAF (page 31) on Sih et al. 2001 (Am J Vet Res 62(9):1500-6), an 18-month study of high cholecalciferol intake in cats. None of the three standards gives a D2 maximum. Applying ÷0.70 would treat a measure of vitamin D status as a safety ratio and allow D2 up to 10,714.3 to 10,742.9 IU/Mcal (about 43,000 IU/kg DM at 4 kcal/g DM), above every cat maximum the three standards print per kg DM or per 1,000 kcal. 10,714.3 is 7,500 ÷0.70: 7,500 IU/1,000 kcal ME is the cat nutritional maximum in the FEDIAF Nutritional Guidelines, publication September 2025 (Table III-4b, page 19; 3,000 IU/100 g DM on page 31), used by the four FEDIAF cat requirements. 10,742.9 is 7,520 ÷0.70: 7,520 IU/1,000 kcal ME is the cat maximum in the 2026 AAFCO Official Publication (page 177; 30,080 IU/kg DM on page 174), used by the two AAFCO cat requirements, and the 2006 NRC cat safe upper limit of 188 micrograms cholecalciferol per 1,000 kcal (Tables 15-10, 15-12 and 15-14, pages 365, 367 and 369; 1 microgram = 40 IU), used by the four NRC cat requirements. Both figures are rounded; the rounding is clinically insignificant and far beyond any measurable precision. This checker therefore holds D2 to the same published maximum as D3. The cost: a D2 intake near the maximum may read higher than it needs to. For dogs and cats, the vitamin D maximum applies to D2, D3, or their combination, as the safest reading: the 2006 NRC (pages 200-205) gives no D2-specific safe upper limit. This checker does not compute D3 + D2: for cats, check the D3 on the Vitamin D (D2 +D3) row plus the D2 on this row against this maximum (see note n262). Dogs enter total vitamin D (D2 + D3) on the Vitamin D (D2 +D3) row, so its maximum already applies to the combination.

text: No automatic adjustment is made to vitamin E concentrations for high PUFA diets which the 2006 NRC recommends increasing in high PUFA diets. See p. 208 for Table 8-2 and the Muggli 1994 proposed formula to calculate if of interest and/or sources of PUFAs requiring high amounts of additional vitamin E are not already fortified like fish oils rich in EPA and DHA. Also see the possible impact of increased vitamin E on vitamin K in Delaney and Dzanis 2018 DOI: 10.2460/javma.252.5.537 . The 2026 AAFCO indicates for dogs (pages 165 and 167), "A diet containing 50 IU of vitamin E will have a ratio >=0.6:1 when the PUFA content is 83 grams or less. Diets containing more than 83 grams of PUFA should contain an additional 0.6 IU of vitamin E for every gram of PUFA." and for cats (pages 175 and 177), "Add 10 IU vitamin E above the minimum concentration for each gram of fish oil per kilogram of diet." AAFCO's dog figures of 50 IU and 83 grams are amounts per kg of dry matter: 50 IU/kg DM is its dog vitamin E minimum in the dry matter table (page 164), given as 12.5 IU per 1,000 kcal ME in its other table (page 166) at its presumed 4,000 kcal ME/kg DM, so 83 grams of PUFA per kg DM is about 20.8 g per 1,000 kcal ME. The 2006 NRC tables give vitamin E in mg alpha-tocopherol, with the footnote 1 IU = 1 mg all-rac-alpha-tocopheryl acetate (footnotes to Tables 15-3, 15-5, 15-8, 15-10, 15-12 and 15-14, pages 358, 360, 363, 365, 367 and 369, referring to its Chapter 8), and this checker uses the NRC mg as IU one to one (this checker's choice, following that footnote); for dogs this fits the 2006 NRC adequate intake of 24 IU per 4,000 kcal (page 209), the 6.0 mg per 1,000 kcal of Tables 15-3, 15-5 and 15-8 (pages 358, 360 and 363). In IU per mg, relative to all-rac-alpha-tocopheryl acetate (1.00), the 2006 NRC (page 207) gives all-rac-alpha-tocopherol 1.10, RRR-alpha-tocopheryl acetate 1.36, RRR-alpha-tocopherol (the naturally occurring form) 1.49, all-rac-alpha-tocopheryl succinate 0.89 and RRR-alpha-tocopheryl succinate 1.21 (United States Pharmacopeia 1985, largely from studies in rats; not measured in dogs or cats); FEDIAF Sept. 2025 Table VII-14 (page 63) gives the same factors for the alcohol and acetate forms. Enter vitamin E in IU: multiply the mg of a stated form by its factor (e.g., 10 mg RRR-alpha-tocopherol is 14.9 IU). No vitamin E maximum is used here, as none of the three standards sets one, so the range high is the min times the row's multiplier (4) and values above it fall in the top band (range-d10). The 2006 NRC states that there is no information on vitamin E toxicity in dogs, that Hall et al. (2003) gave dogs 447 mg all-rac-tocopheryl acetate for 17 weeks with no adverse effects (no basis, such as per kg diet, is printed for this amount) and that the NRC (1987) suggested a maximum tolerable level of 1,000 to 2,000 IU/kg diet (page 209). For cats it reports dose-related toxicity of vitamin E injected into kittens from birth to 3 weeks of age (no deaths at about 20 mg/kg BW/day, significant mortality at 100 to 200 mg/kg BW/day and death of all kittens at 1,000 mg/kg BW/day; Phelps 1981; the 2006 NRC also describes the injected doses as about 50 to 1,000 mg/kg BW/day, a range the 20 mg/kg BW/day figure lies below: an inconsistency in NRC's text, kept here as printed) and prolonged clotting times, restored by vitamin K therapy, in cats fed fish-based diets fortified with vitamin E (Strieker et al. 1996), and it concludes that the data do not allow a safe upper limit of vitamin E to be defined (pages 209 and 210). The 2026 AAFCO records that the dog vitamin E maximum was deleted from its profiles because the 2006 NRC had set no safe upper limit, having no information on vitamin E toxicity in dogs (page 173). See also Delaney and Dzanis 2018 on the possible impact of increased vitamin E on vitamin K (DOI: 10.2460/javma.252.5.537).

text: Carbohydrate maximum based on protein and fat minimums when no carb max is defined is calculated. The high range is calculated as (1000 kcal - ((min protein g/Mcal * 4 kcal/g protein) + (min fat g/Mcal *9 kcal/ g fat)))/4 kcal/g carbohydrate. For example, if protein min g/Mcal = 25 and fat min g/Mcal= 13.8, using the Atwater energy conversion factors of 4 kcal/g protein and 9 kcal/g fat, the minimum amount of calories from protein and fat would be 224.2 kcal (25*4 = 100; 13.8 * 9 = 124.2; 100+124.2 = 224.2); 1000 kcal per Mcal - 224.2 = 775.8 kcal maximally from carbohydrate; 775.8/4 kcal/g carb. = 193.95 g/Mcal max from carb. The protein and fat mins used are those of the Protein and Fat rows, including any raise for a caloric restriction or a low energy fed (protein only; see notes n192 and n214) and the AAFCO dry matter factor (see note n180). When they alone supply 1000 kcal per Mcal or more, the calculated max is 0 instead of a negative number: 0 means the protein and fat minimums alone supply all the energy, and the carbohydrate min (see note n288) is then above this max.

text: Set at 3.5 kcal/g dry matter (DM) based on the lowest historical threshold in some regulatory guidelines (pre-2016 AAFCO Official Publications (dog profiles)) to switch to using requirements on a dry matter basis instead of an energy basis when a food's energy density is below this value. It is this checker's own minimum, not an energy density requirement of the 2006 NRC, 2026 AAFCO, or FEDIAF Sept. 2025, and neither is this row's fixed 6 kcal/g DM range high (see note n301). The 2026 AAFCO dog and cat profiles presume 4000 kcal ME/kg DM (4 kcal/g DM) and state that "formulations less than 4000 kcal ME/kg should not be corrected for energy" (Footnote a on pages 164 and 175; page 183 states the same rule), so AAFCO compares such foods, whatever their moisture, with its dry matter values without energy correction. This checker compares every food per Mcal, which matches the 2006 NRC (page 355) and FEDIAF Sept. 2025 (page 13), as both correct for any energy density. To apply AAFCO's rule under an AAFCO requirement, when the energy density entered (this row's low entry) is above 0 and below 4 kcal/g DM, each min that a caloric restriction raises, and the fat min, is multiplied by 4 divided by that energy density (the AAFCO dry matter factor; see note n180), together with any caloric restriction factor. This equals AAFCO's dry matter comparison to within the rounding between its dry matter and per 1,000 kcal tables: e.g., at 3.6 kcal/g DM the 65 g/Mcal adult cat protein min becomes 72.2 g/Mcal, which is 26% protein in DM. The exception is 7 values that AAFCO prints differently in its two tables (for cats, valine for growth and reproduction, and linoleic acid; for dogs, EPA + DHA, sodium, chloride and selenium for growth and reproduction, and selenium for adult maintenance): for these the factored min corresponds to a dry matter value other than the one AAFCO prints, so a food can meet it here and not AAFCO's dry matter value, or the reverse (see notes n060, n080, n081, n089, n090, n111, n112, n122, n123, n131, n135, n132, n136, n133 and n137). The maximums stay per Mcal, this checker's cautious choice, as an animal eating a less energy-dense food to its energy needs takes in the per Mcal amount; so such a food at an AAFCO dry matter maximum can read above the per Mcal maximum here. Nothing is adjusted when no energy density is entered or it is 4 or more, or under an NRC or FEDIAF requirement. AAFCO adds that formulations of low energy density should not be considered adequate for reproductive needs (dogs) or for growth or reproductive needs (cats) based on comparison to the profiles alone (Footnote a on pages 164 and 175). For reference, the 2026 AAFCO (page 167) states that before the 2016 revisions to its profiles the presumed caloric density for dog foods was 3500 kcal ME/kg DM for nutrient concentrations per kg DM.
